clips.send: Undersea fiber-optic cable. Almost all data between continents travels through cables on the sea floor — not satellites. In deep water a cable is only about as thick as a garden hose. Ships lay it from giant spools. Repeaters every 50–100 km or so boost the light so it can cross a whole ocean.

clips.send: Fiber-optic cable. Glass threads thinner than a hair carry bits as flashes of light. Light in glass travels about 200,000 km per second — Atlanta to Chicago in about 5 ms. One fiber can carry many colours of light at once, each with its own stream of data.

clips.send: The two ends. The sender’s computer uses TCP (a protocol, 协议) to cut data into packets and number them. The receiver puts packets back in order by number and asks again for any that are missing. Each computer on the internet has an IP address such as 203.0.113.7.

clips.send: Wi-Fi radio link. Bits ride on radio waves between your laptop and the router. Walls and distance weaken the signal — that is why Wi-Fi gets slow far from the router. Radio waves move at almost the speed of light: 300,000 km per second.

clips.send: Internet service provider (ISP). Companies like phone and cable companies connect homes and schools to the big “backbone” networks. The ISP’s routers send your packets onto long-distance fiber. The internet is made of tens of thousands of separate networks that agree to pass each other’s packets.

clips.send: A message’s trip. Your message is cut into numbered packets. Each one carries the destination’s IP address, like an envelope. Every router reads the address and sends the packet one hop closer — it never needs to know the whole route. Dashed lines across the ocean are undersea fiber-optic cables. Click any line or router to break or fix it.

clips.send: Your home Wi-Fi router. Wi-Fi sends bits as radio waves (usually 2.4 or 5 GHz) — only across a few rooms. It gives each device at home a local address and shares one internet connection. From here, a cable (copper or fiber) runs to your internet service provider (ISP).

clips.send: Backbone router. A router reads only the address on the packet, checks its routing table and forwards it to the best next hop. If a line breaks, routers tell each other and quickly choose new routes. Big backbone routers forward huge numbers of packets every second.

clips.send: 光纤。比头发还细的玻璃丝用闪烁的光传送比特。。光在玻璃里每秒约走20万千米——从亚特兰大到芝加哥约5毫秒。。一根光纤可以同时传送多种颜色的光，每种颜色都是一路独立的数据。

clips.send: Wi-Fi无线连接。比特“骑”在无线电波上，在电脑和路由器之间往返。。墙壁和距离会让信号变弱——所以离路由器远了，Wi-Fi就会变慢。。无线电波的速度接近光速：每秒30万千米。

clips.send: 通信的两端。发送方的计算机按照TCP协议（protocol）把数据切成数据包并编号。。接收方按编号把数据包重新排好，缺了哪个就请求重发。。互联网上的每台计算机都有一个IP地址，例如203.0.113.7。

clips.send: 主干路由器。路由器只读数据包上的地址，查一下路由表，再把它转发给最合适的“下一跳”。。如果某条线路断了，路由器会互相通知，很快改走别的路线。。大型主干路由器每秒要转发数量惊人的数据包。

clips.send: 家里的无线路由器。Wi-Fi用无线电波（通常是2.4或5 GHz）传送比特——只能覆盖几个房间。。它给家里每台设备分配一个本地地址，大家共用一条宽带。。从这里开始，一根线缆（铜线或光纤）通到网络服务商（ISP）。

clips.send: 一条消息的旅程。你的消息被切成带编号的数据包，每个数据包上都写着目的地的IP地址，就像信封上的地址。。每个 路由器读一下地址，把数据包向终点再送近“一跳”——它不需要知道整条路线。。横跨大洋的虚线是海底光缆。点击任何一条线或一个路由器，可以把它弄坏或修好。

clips.send: 互联网服务提供商（ISP）。电信、有线电视等公司把家庭和学校接入大型“主干网”。。网络服务商的路由器把你的数据包送上长途光纤。。互联网由成千上万个独立的网络组成，它们约定互相转发数据包。

clips.send: 海底光缆。洲与洲之间的数据几乎都通过铺在海底的光缆传送——而不是卫星。。在深海里，一条光缆只有花园水管那么粗，由专门的布缆船从巨大的线盘上放下去。。大约每隔50—100千米有一个中继器，把光信号放大，让它能跨越整个大洋。
